Migration is triggered by an exponential timer at each queue; upon expiration, a job departs and travels through a random route before returning. This model, which encompasses the Multi-Server Multi-Family Queueing Network as a specific instance, is analyzed under the condition that the migration pattern remains constant. Leveraging uniformization, we demonstrate that the joint stationary distribution corresponds to that of a standard queueing network with constant routing probabilities. This finding enables the analysis of queues with time-varying routing via approximation by networks with constant routing, thereby facilitating the performance evaluation of this queueing system. The paper concludes by presenting numerical simulations that validate this theoretical framework. Migration models find applications in various domains, including call centers, cloud computing, and job scheduling, often characterized by a large number of queues and a high volume of customers. Given the theoretical and practical significance of migration, this topic warrants further research. Specifically, in scenarios involving many queues and few servers, it would be valuable to determine if an asymptotic regime exists where migration's impact diminishes. Additionally, as the paper notes, migration introduces a time delay in the queueing network; an interesting alternative approach would be to model this delay using service resumption rather than migration. Furthermore, given the need for efficient algorithms to compute stationary distributions, research could also explore methods to accelerate these computations. The proposed methodology introduces an alternative algorithm for migration-based network approximation, grounded in the theoretical results of this work. Additionally, numerical experiments indicate that the algorithm for calculating the stationary distribution is effective for networks with a moderate number of queues. For large networks, we suggest that approximations using constant routing probabilities serve as a useful initial guess for solving the migration problem. Additionally, uniformization techniques can be integrated with other approaches to further enhance the accuracy of these approximations. Finally, an interesting direction for future research involves extending this methodology to migration patterns with a finite number of loops. The current work focuses on migration with an infinite loop, although finitary migration is more pertinent to real-world applications. Additionally, it would be interesting to investigate whether this approach can be extended to migration models with large delays. This study introduces a method for migration in queueing networks alongside a method for computing the stationary distribution, representing a novel contribution to the field. We believe these findings will have a positive impact on the queueing theory community and related fields. Our results indicate that, prior to compression, silica molecules in the nanowires are organized in an alternating pattern relative to the stress axis. Under compressive loading, these molecules reorganize to establish a more compact and regular arrangement. This increased compactness facilitates the formation of compression-induced plasticity (CIP) through the ordering of free silicate ions, while simultaneously destabilizing the plasticity-induced void (PIV) mechanism, which relies on a less compact molecular configuration. The competition between the CIP and PIV mechanisms ultimately governs the compressive strength and the density of compression-induced voids in the nanowires. This study elucidates the atomic-scale processes occurring under uniaxial compression in silica nanowires, offering valuable insights for the design and optimization of nanostructured silica materials for plasticity and void formation. Furthermore, the proposed design strategy aims to enhance the impact resistance, toughness, and self-healing capabilities of nanostructured silica materials. The findings from this research are applicable to various silicate-based nanostructures, such as zeolites. Additionally, this study was conducted as a student research experience program. holes within four-dimensional higher derivative gravity, which includes a general combination of Einstein, Maxwell, and topological Lovelock terms. These solutions maintain a circular profile and are defined by a set of degenerate horizons. We provide a detailed analysis of their properties and geometry, outlining the conditions necessary for their stability. Furthermore, we explore the limit where the Lovelock parameter approaches zero and compare key features with those of standard Einstein-Maxwell black holes. Finally, we calculate thermodynamic variables and examine the behavior of heat capacity and entropy, ultimately investigating the microstructure and information content associated with higher derivative horizons. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the nature of these black holes and aligns with recent investigations into modified gravity frameworks. Additionally, we investigate the equation of state, phase transitions, and critical parameters, finding that the law resembles that of van der Waals fluids. Consequently, we conclude that modified Lovelock gravity enables the formation of information-rich black holes. As the spin and momentum increase, the black hole develops a complex internal structure, while entropy rises as the charge increases, converging to standard General Relativity results when the charge is zero. These findings offer valuable insights into the internal composition and stability of such black holes, enhancing our grasp of black hole physics. We anticipate that this work will be valuable for investigating modified gravity theories and for future theoretical and observational research. No conflicts of interest exist. in artificial intelligence (AI) have sparked significant interest in its ethical implications. As AI becomes embedded in various societal sectors, it introduces new ethical challenges, necessitating that developers, practitioners, and organizations prioritize moral considerations. However, the lack of established guidelines for these considerations hinders the effective enforcement of ethical standards. This study aims to offer a comprehensive analysis of AI ethics by examining relevant literature and applying the Delphi method to identify key factors. The results indicate that organizational and individual issues are the primary drivers of unethical AI behavior, while the consequences largely undermine trust in AI systems and outputs. Given that unethical behavior stems from a combination of intentional and unintentional actions, this research also seeks to clarify the distinctions and similarities between these two types. By clarifying the sources of unethical behavior and the resulting outcomes, this study provides insights for stakeholders to formulate effective solutions to ethical problems within AI. We introduce a generic small-step reduction relation that can unify various operational semantics, big-step transitions, and hybrid models where certain transitions are atomic while others are not. Furthermore, we establish verification conditions ensuring that hybrid small-step semantics preserve big-step assertions. Consequently, any program proven correct under big-step semantics remains correct when utilizing hybrid small-step transition systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that small-step verification is more straightforward than hybrid verification because compact data-flow assertions suffice for proving small-step correctness, whereas big-step or hybrid correctness often necessitates more complex behaviorally oriented validity invariants and IO-closing rules. This observation is supported by a comparative study of small-step versus hybrid verification, conducted by rewriting mIRC—a mutable reference language—with various small-step semantics and validating three such implementations using Coq. In this process, we also identified several practical verification challenges that arise when small-step semantics include non-atomic transitions or mIRC-like mutable semantics, challenges that are either absent or significantly reduced in small-step implementations. In these instances, small-step verification is as simple as verification under purely big-step semantics, which has been previously shown to yield concise and elegant proofs. Gödel and Döring demonstrated that every primitive recursive function is representable. This note establishes that any function at Level Three of the Hardy hierarchy is also representable. Furthermore, we prove that representability aligns precisely with provability in Peano Arithmetic for these specific functions; consequently, any function not representable also cannot be proven to be representable by Peano Arithmetic. Finally, after converting function symbols into logical formulas, every representable function is shown to be semantically deducible from the first-order prime number theorem. Therefore, the first-order prime number theorem can be utilized as a semantic tool to ascertain the mathematical deducibility of functions within Peano Arithmetic. Any function for which such a proof is unfeasible serves as a demonstration that the theorem's capacity to prove mathematical deducibility extends beyond primitive recursive functions. Finally, it is demonstrated that the polynomial time complexity of the inverse function $J^{-1}$ (related to the Ackermann function by De Bruijn's notation) is unprovable in Peano Arithmetic, thereby providing a solution to Berry's Paradox within the context of mathematical logic. This finding also constitutes a solution to Goodman's Paradox regarding the indescribability of complexity. It follows that Goodman's Paradox remains unresolved by first-order number theory. of light traversing it, a phenomenon recognized as the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect, where the displacement scales with the medium's velocity. In this article, we present an experimental investigation of the inverse effect, defined as optical induced shift, in which the medium remains stationary while the optical path is displaced in the opposite direction by a phase-conjugated beam. We measure an average displacement of $20\,\mu\rm{m}$, which exhibits no dependence on temperature variations or environmental vibrations. Among potential explanations, we favor an experimental artifact stemming from the displacement of the sample within a phase conjugator caused by heating. This spurious effect can be mitigated by either applying water cooling to the optical induced shift sample or utilizing water-cooled phase conjugators for all other beams, thereby validating the experimental protocol for observing the reverse Fresnel-Fizeau effect. Consequently, the genuine reverse effect must be smaller than the measured value. To date, this phenomenon, first theorized by Feynman in 1956, remains unobserved. A valid demonstration of this fundamental relativistic effect could serve as a pedagogical tool to clarify the principles of special relativity and the constancy of the speed of light. Furthermore, it may inspire new optical technologies and creative artistic endeavors. (See the Supplemental Material for color figures and additional artistic examples.) Our findings also hold potential applications in optical tweezers and optical trapping. The binary nature of the uncertainty results in a uncertainty set $\Delta$ that lacks regular polynomial-size representations, such as ellipsoids or simplexes. This study adapts the dual decomposition technique to the task of finding extremal parameter realizations, demonstrating its efficacy through applications to robust mixed-integer linear programming (IMLP) and robust mixed-integer quadratic programming (IMQP). Extensive computational experiments highlight the method's effectiveness. Furthermore, the study establishes theoretical guarantees for the proposed algorithm's convergence. These results are derived by developing a new duality theory for the search for extreme parameter realizations, which features a dual with significant practical implications. The new dual not only ensures the algorithm's convergence but also yields a general duality result: the objective value of a robust optimization problem with $\Delta$ defined over binary variables equals the parameter $\theta$ of a certain auxiliary robust-combinatorial problem with a simpler structure, where $\theta^2 \geq \theta^1$ for any compact $\Delta$. This allows the exact approach to be utilized in broad scenarios. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of this new duality. Experimental findings indicate that the approach is particularly advantageous when the dimension $n$ of the underlying space is small, while remaining effective in higher-dimensional scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm identifies parameter realizations where constraint qualifications typically fail. These realizations are critical for characterizing the structure of robust optimization sets, offering insights into the typical tightness of constraints within the $\text{conv}(\Delta)$-convex hull of $\Delta$. These insights facilitate the search for tighter outer approximations and provide a foundation for the validity of the strong duality result. Additionally, the algorithm can determine the $\nu$-robust rank, a concept recently proposed to analyze the structure of robust optimization. This capability is especially valuable in scenarios where the $\Delta$-convex hull is not tight, a common situation in robust IMLP and IMQP. Furthermore, the algorithm can compute the $\infty$-robust rank, a concept defined in [18], which is effective for problems with an ellipsoidal uncertainty set $\Delta$. These robust ranks are also applicable to sensitivity analysis in robust optimization. Overall, the paper presents a new algorithm with multiple applications. However, GNN performance degrades significantly when nodes possess an excessive number of incident edges, a condition known as high-degree nodehood (HDN). This issue is particularly prevalent in real-world applications, such as modeling social networks where individuals may have hundreds of connections. This paper provides a comprehensive review of GNNs under HDN across supervised and unsupervised learning frameworks. In the supervised domain, we detail techniques for handling both transductive and predictive settings. Within the transductive framework, we examine preprocessing methods that reconstruct the local neighborhood of high-degree nodes and modify message-passing strategies without altering the model's core architecture. Conversely, in the predictive framework, we investigate low-pass filtering methods applied during message passing, followed by a discussion of approaches designed to generate low-degree subgraphs for training and testing. Finally, for the unsupervised context, we present methods focused on graph representation learning through the reconstruction of edge links. To support this review, we provide a public repository containing 14 experimental graphs and a Python codebase implementing preprocessing strategies and low-pass filtering approaches for supervised low-degree learning. We term this collection the "GNN-Unfolded" repository to honor the foundational GNN-folded codebase. Our aim with this paper and repository is to offer a thorough overview of current strategies for addressing HDN and to advance future research in low-degree learning. We conclude by outlining existing limitations and proposing new directions for low-degree GNN research. The code will be accessible at: https://github.com/GNN-Unfolded-GitHub. *Equal Contribution.*

Set disjointness with promise demands two parties to determine if the sets they possess are disjoint or if one is contained within the other; in contrast, the disjointness promise requires verification only when the sets are identical. We demonstrate that, under a linear threshold promise, the randomized (including LOCC) quantum communication complexity of the disjointness promise is $O(\sqrt{n}\log n)$, where $n$ represents the number of elements in the sets. This result leverages the connection between quantum communication complexity and quantum information theory, specifically the quantum chromatic number of a graph. Notably, this approach is constructive, implying efficient quantum states and operations. In comparison, Bravyi's non-constructive method utilizes only one-qubit gates. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n}/\text{polylog}(n))$ for the quantum communication complexity of the disjointness promise. The primary proof technique involves reducing a quantum state preparation challenge to the disjointness promise and demonstrating a quantum lower bound for this reduction, which is proved via a quantum arithmetic circuit complexity result. This finding is likely of independent interest. The connection to quantum information is grounded in Bravyi's work, while the non-constructive aspect is derived from his results. Our approach is also influenced by Bravyi's non-constructive proof for the quantum communication complexity of the disjointness promise. This work introduces a broader theoretical approach that encompasses correlated and/or noncrystalline systems, deriving both linear and nonlinear Hall conductivities from the many-electron anomalous velocity. The results obtained for independent electrons emerge as specific instances of this general formalism. To illustrate the framework's capabilities, we apply it to a general one-dimensional model of noncrystalline interacting particles. In this context, we calculate the nonlinear Hall conductivity for a current induced by an electric field gradient, identifying it as an particle-hole anomalous velocity. This phenomenon stems from a topological invariant defined via a Berry connection in frequency space, which governs the interband nonlinear response between single-particle bands. This invariant is analogous to the frequency-momentum invariant that defines a "hydrodynamic" Chern number in a time-varying one-dimensional system. Additionally, in the one-dimensional case, we demonstrate that all contributions to the Hall nonlinear response derived from many-body anomalous velocities can be expressed as total derivatives of specific many-body adiabatic response functions. These response functions are closely related to interacting generalizations of the Berry connection and curvature in crystal momentum and frequency spaces. For uncorrelated electrons, this formulation precisely recovers the nonlinear Hall effect described by the "hydrodynamic" Chern number. Finally, in the one-body limit, the general nonlinear Hall conductivity reduces to the conventional nonlinear Hall effect, where it is identified with the second-order Berry curvature of Bloch states. Overall, our findings reveal that particle-hole nonlinear Hall effects in one-dimensional systems represent an adiabatic manifestation of the "hydrodynamic" Chern number, a concept that may extend to higher dimensions. Such effects could be observed in one-dimensional chains of interacting atoms exhibiting spin-orbit coupling, which are commonly manipulated in cold-atom experiments. Furthermore, these results may aid in identifying nonlinear Hall signatures in other low-dimensional systems, including photonic topological insulators and other noncrystalline structures. This note provides a comprehensive classification of the groups (up to isomorphism) that function as deck transformation groups for iterates of such bicritical rational maps, thereby extending findings from a prior publication by the authors. We present a method for training robust classifiers using distribution-free, out-of-support adversarial training, which demonstrates marked improvements when a robust surrogate model is employed. These modifications enable us to broaden our technique to support distribution-free retraining across a wider range of datasets. This paper introduces the UC Solver 2.0, a novel branch-and-cut algorithm incorporating column generation. By utilizing column generation techniques, the solver separates variables through a start-up cost-based heuristic. Additionally, several cutting planes are implemented to eliminate infeasible time periods associated with prohibited zones and minimum generation limits. These plans include big-M constraints enforcing generation limits, removing infeasible timetables; minimum up/down time constraints within a time-period context; and minimum generation limits. These models rely on the assumption that the treated unit is an observationally equivalent combination of the control units. However, this assumption may fail if the treatment effect is heterogeneous and varies non-linearly based on unit-specific covariates. In such non-linear scenarios, the treated unit may not be representable by a linear combination of the controls, causing standard SC methods to bias the causal effect estimate because the linear approximation of the treated unit deviates from reality. To address issues arising from non-linear relationships between unit covariates and treatment effects, we propose the Piecewise Linear Synthetic Control (PLSC) method. PLSC divides the treatment effect into several pieces and constructs the treated unit non-linearly using linear combinations of control units. Under weaker assumptions, PLSC yields a more accurate representation of the treated unit compared to traditional SC methods. Furthermore, under conditions where the treatment effect is piecewise linear regarding unit covariates, PLSC can exactly represent the treated unit without bias. We also present two tests for PLSC to assess the validity of the piecewise linear assumption against the traditional linear assumption for robustness. Finally, we apply PLSC to evaluate the causal impact of large-scale earthquakes on Japanese municipalities and reveal additional insights into how the treatment effect varies non-linearly with respect to covariates. This paper introduces a novel framework for identifying similarity classes of unlabeled graphs based on structural characteristics. Our approach builds on the foundational concept that the kernel kernel($G$) of a graph $G$—defined as the shortest path distance matrix between isomorphic nodes in $G$—can partition the collection of all unlabeled graphs into distinct similarity classes. For any two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$, we demonstrate that they belong to the same similarity class if and only if they share identical kernel eigenspaces across every frequency $f \in \mathbb{N}$. We establish the transitivity of this relation to validate the formation of equivalence classes. Our methodology utilizes kernel eigenspaces to identify shared similarity traits among unlabelled graphs. By integrating these eigenspaces, we construct a feature embedding for graph objects, enabling the visualization and identification of similarities among them. The efficacy and validity of this framework are further supported by its successful application as a machine learning feature. Specifically, we train a deep neural network using these kernel-based features as input to forecast the graph edit distance between a given graph pair. Through comprehensive experiments and analysis, we confirm the efficacy and validity of this feature-driven approach. Furthermore, we release an open-source software package implementing all proposed algorithms and experiments, facilitating future research and development. To ensure reproducibility, all code is accessible via the provided link. Additionally, we have developed a web-based interactive visualization tool for these features. The paper concludes with final remarks and suggestions for future work. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study on using kernel-based features for visualizing graph similarities. This deluge of data will produce two primary byproducts: an extensive catalog of GW transients and a set of inferences regarding the cosmological make-up of the universe, specifically redshift and matter density. These redshifts will offer a unique method for mapping the large-scale structure of the galaxy, while the Hubble parameter ($H(z)$) will be constrained using GW-standard siren measurements. Both the redshift and Hubble parameter estimates will face a significant challenge from Gaussian and non-Gaussian systematic errors inherent to this new measurement technique. In this study, we outline the sources of these systematic errors and propose methods to mitigate them. We introduce a novel Bayesian framework that integrates these errors directly into the analysis of large-scale structure and cosmological constraints derived from GW standard siren observations. This new approach demonstrates initial success in identifying potential sources of systematic errors within a mock catalog of GW transients. Furthermore, we show how these errors can be detected by examining residuals in siren observations when compared against analyses that ignore such errors. Finally, we discuss the implications of these systematic errors on the constraints expected from future observations. The code implementing these methods is available on GitHub. When such a cover exists, the covering number $\sigma(R)$ denotes the cardinality of a minimal cover. A ring $R$ is defined as $\sigma$-elementary if $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$. This paper presents the first instances of $\sigma$-elementary rings $R$ possessing a nontrivial Jacobson radical $J$ such that the quotient $R/J$ is noncommutative, and it establishes the covering numbers for these rings. Furthermore, the study provides the covering numbers for several classes of $\sigma$-elementary rings that are quotients of matrix rings or group rings. These findings address previously established open questions and offer the initial examples demonstrating how the covering numbers of rings can decrease when passing to quotients. Additionally, the paper lists the covering numbers for various collections of Artinian rings. Notably, for a nonunital simple ring $S$, we have $\sigma(S) < \sigma(S/I)$ for every nonzero ideal $I$, and for any Artinian ring $R$, $\sigma(R) \leq \sigma(R/\operatorname{Nil}(R))$, where $\operatorname{Nil}(R)$ represents the set of nilpotent elements in $R$. These results contrast with established behaviors in other algebraic structures, such as the case where a finite subset $M$ of a vector space $V$ forms a maximal proper linear subspace and $\dim V \geq 4$, in which case $\dim V/M' > \dim V/M$ for all proper subspaces $M'$. Consequently, these findings provide counterexamples to analogous hypotheses proposed for rings. Finally, the paper includes families of rings that admit no cover of any cardinality less than or equal to 8. These families include certain Artinian rings formed as direct sums of three or more indecomposable ideals, as well as specific Artinian rings over finite fields that are quotients of matrix rings over finite commutative local rings. For the latter, the covering number is exactly 9. These findings have also been incorporated into the author's monograph titled "Rings with Minimal Covers," published by De Gruyter in 2022. Unlike translation surfaces, the directional flow on dilation surfaces can contain trajectories that accumulate on limit cycles; these are closed geodesics termed hyperbolic due to the nontrivial homothety they induce. A longstanding conjecture posits that a dilation surface lacking any hyperbolic closed geodesics is essentially a translation surface. Under the assumption that a dilation surface possesses a horocycle (a direction in which the flow is purely translational), this conjecture is proven, yielding several corollaries and confirming a specific instance of Satake's conjecture originally proposed in 1958. The proof utilizes numerous concepts and tools from non-positively curved geometry and Lie groups, demonstrating the significant interplay between dilation surfaces and these geometric structures. Notably, the analysis of a model dilation surface featuring a translational direction reveals that its geodesic flow exhibits negative curvature, stands topologically conjugate to the geodesic flow of a rank one simple Lie group, and displays dynamical properties linked to ideal triangles. Furthermore, the relationship between homotheties and the rank of geodesics provides deeper insight into the dilation surface's dynamics. Additionally, the study of hyperbolic closed geodesics employs ideas regarding matrix discreteness and the connection to pinched horocyclic maps. The model dilation surface's topological conjugacy to a specific Lie group's geodesic flow offers a distinct approach to understanding the connections between dilation surfaces and this geometric framework. Moreover, the application of pinched horocyclic maps to analyze the dynamics of hyperbolic closed geodesics on the dilation surface further underscores this rich geometric connection. Collectively, these findings prove that a dilation surface possessing a horocycle is quasi-isometric to a non-positively curved Lie group, thereby substantiating the proof of Satake's conjecture and advancing the understanding of this intricate relationship. This study aims to determine whether such a system can form a planet and, if so, what the resulting planet-mass distribution looks like. Using a radiative hydrodynamic (RDH) code, we simulate the gas flow within a typical gap system featuring a 1.5 Jupiter mass (Mj) disk with a 0.54 au cavity radius ($Rc$). This configuration aligns with both theoretical predictions and existing observations. We establish the conditions necessary to fill the cavity and simulate gas deposition to drive sedimentation of dust particles. Our results indicate that these cavities can be filled, though it requires a few hundred orbital timescales. Once filled, we analyze particle deposition to estimate the distribution of the solid phase resulting from sedimentation. These sediments are then transported radially outward via aerodynamic drag. Comparing our findings with observations of young stars, we observe that in regions where the cavity can form (where $\Sigma_0 R_0 > 1.5$ M$\odot$/au), the transport timescale for solids to reach outer areas ($Rc + 10$ au) can be as short as a few orbital timescales. Our simulations suggest that in such a system, the distribution of planet masses formed through cavity filling follows a power law with an exponent of approximately -1.5 and a maximum mass of roughly 0.005 Mj. Additionally, we estimate the stellar mass accumulation rate to be $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ M$\odot$/yr. This rate is comparable to accretion rates derived from H$\alpha$ emission in T Tauri stars, suggesting that cavities may be more prevalent in the local star-forming region than previously thought. Finally, we propose that the gas accretion mechanism is also applicable to the core accretion model, offering an alternative explanation for the gas excess observed in some disks. In conclusion, the presence of an inner cavity in a protoplanetary disk offers a promising solution to the "gas excess" problem. However, further research is required to fully understand the physical mechanisms of planet formation. This work also

This simplified model assumes spherical particles with a Gaussian distribution representing the jet's cross-sectional area, utilizing randomly oriented vectors formed from two orthogonal unit vectors, $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the amplitude of the magnetic field in the ambient medium and the turbulence timescale within the jet's travel path are critical factors in determining the AGN jet's structure. Finally, we find that the magnitude of linear polarization increases with the density of the ambient medium. These findings provide valuable insights for interpreting real-world observations of AGN jets. The proposed methodology represents a valuable, general tool for future studies aiming to extract physical information from Stokes parameters. Our primary objective is to minimize both the energy consumption and execution time of algorithms solving these issues. We present randomized algorithms that achieve optimal performance for both naming and counting on networks of $n$ stations, with a running time of $O(n \log n)$ and an energy complexity of $O(\log n)$. Additionally, we propose algorithms with linear running time, denoted as $t_n$. These linear algorithms are not only optimal for naming but also provide an $O(\log n)$ approximation for counting. Specifically, we define $k_n$ as the minimal running time for solving the naming problem and demonstrate that our algorithms operate with a time complexity of $k_n \left(1 + \frac{1}{\rho} + O\left(\frac{1}{\rho^2}\right)\right)$, where $\rho = \frac{c-1}{4}$ and $c$ represents the channel's expansion. Furthermore, we establish that this approach is optimal for naming. The analysis of $k_n$ is also relevant to the counting problem, as we can formulate it as $k_n \rho \left(1 + O\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\right)\right)$. In this context, we prove an upper bound of $2k_n$ and a lower bound of $\frac{5}{9}k_n$, both of which are tight. The value of $k_n$ was first identified by Gasieniec et al. in the context of single-hop beeping networks. Their work demonstrated that a randomized algorithm with deterministic energy complexity can solve naming in $k_n$ time with high probability. They also showed that $k_n$ grows logarithmically and provided upper and lower bounds. In this study, we utilize a version of $k_n$ derived from a randomized algorithm with stochastic energy complexity. We demonstrate that this growth behavior is optimal when considering trade-offs between time and energy. The primary contributions of this research are the establishment of new bounds for $k_n$ and the provision of optimal algorithms for naming and counting that minimize the costs associated with time and energy. Leveraging the unique capabilities of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), this study demonstrates that the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) is maximized within the antiferromagnetic but not the nematic region. Specifically, in the parent compound $\text{BaFe}_2(\text{As}_{1-x}\text{Po}_x)_2$, where NMR is driven by a substantial hole spin susceptibility and significant hyperfine coupling, antiferromagnetic order produces a clear spin gap in $T_1$. This finding supports an N=2 node structure for the superconducting spin gap, indicating an $s^{++}$ pairing state modulated by two Fermi surface "mountains." Conversely, within the nematic region, $T_c$ follows the Pauli limit, implying that Pauli limiting governs the upper bound of $T_c$ and suggesting an $s^{\pm}$ + $d$-wave pairing state. This result clarifies that the spin gap size is controlled by antiferromagnetic fluctuations rather than nematicity, aligning with earlier theoretical predictions and ruling out exotic pairing states like $s^{\pm}$ + $p$. Overall, the study establishes a robust quantitative link between spin fluctuations, pairing symmetry, and $T_c$ in FeSCs via a direct measurement of the spin gap. These findings are also examined in relation to other FeSC families. By utilizing compounds with varying hole densities as a proxy for temperature, this work provides definitive evidence of a first-order phase transition at $T_c$ in $\text{BaFe}_2(\text{As}_{1-x}\text{Po}_x)_2$. Furthermore, it reveals two distinct spin gap regimes: a "two-step" recovery in the antiferromagnetic region and an exponential recovery in the nematic region. These findings strongly suggest that a bosonic mechanism, analogous to that observed in cuprates, is also present in FeSCs. Finally, the study confirms that a BCS-like spin response is inherent to FeSCs and underscores the critical role of Fermi surface shape in determining the spin gap response. This collection, referred to as the {\it Babylonian Locus}, consists of projections \cc{p}2 where the projection center lies respectively above, below, or alongside the center above side of the plane. We demonstrate that this family possesses non-trivial topological complexity \cc{p}2. Following a recent polynomial-time key recovery attack that compromises the original system in specific scenarios, we propose two defensive strategies. Firstly, incorporating an affine transformation between the public and private spaces serves as a proven method to thwart known key recovery attacks on code-based cryptosystems. Secondly, integrating a syndrome decoder into the decryption algorithm functions as a standard defense against key recovery, applicable to both code-based and Goppa schemes. We demonstrate that integrating an affine transformation with a masked syndrome decoder significantly enhances security compared to the original Loidreau scheme, thereby improving its resilience against current key recovery threats. Additionally, we address the high decryption complexity introduced by the affine transformation, which stems from the enlarged public code. We identify two potential solutions for this issue and recommend the less resource-intensive approach. Through parameter analysis using the introduced metrics, we illustrate that the proposed scheme offers superior security and performance relative to the original Loidreau scheme. Finally, we evaluate the security of our scheme against existing attacks specific to code-based systems. Furthermore, we outline the criteria for selecting parameters to ensure robust security while maintaining reasonable efficiency. Our analysis indicates that these selections offer adequate protection against current attacks while achieving reasonable performance metrics. All findings are supported by comprehensive numerical evaluations. In conclusion, this work represents a critical step toward the realization of post-quantum cryptographic systems. This study investigates this capability within few-shot classification, where models must achieve high accuracy using only a few labeled examples. Specifically, we train PLMs like BERT and RoBERTa using supervised few-shot learning (SFSL) and evaluate their performance in zero-shot classification against an information-theoretic bound derived from mutual information (MI) to quantify feature informativeness. Furthermore, to enhance zero-shot transfer, we propose randomly masking tokens during training to encourage the model to retain critical information from previously unseen training data, thereby further improving its final evaluation metrics. This paper offers valuable insights into the few-shot adaptation capabilities of PLMs and provides empirical evidence to guide their training strategies. Nevertheless, FL is susceptible to privacy breaches via inference attacks, where adversaries attempt to reconstruct private information from shared model updates. This study investigates privacy risks within FL by adopting a comprehensive perspective that accounts for varying levels of access a potential attacker might possess. Specifically, we examine both black-box and white-box scenarios to develop novel inference attack methods capable of reconstructing private data. Our proposed attack achieves state-of-the-art performance by successfully recovering private information, including digital fingerprints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these results remain robust even in resource-constrained environments characterized by a limited number of participating users. We validate the efficacy of our methodology across multiple practical FL applications, such as spam filtering and voice recognition. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets, including CIFAR-10 and MNIST, show that our attack outperforms existing techniques by up to 20%. To our knowledge, this work offers one of the most thorough and powerful analyses of both black-box and white-box inference attacks targeting private data in federated learning. necessitates a comprehensive and precise understanding of the urban environment. However, the complex nature of modern cities renders such environmental perception a difficult challenge, a bottleneck that must be overcome to enable safe autonomous navigation for smart city vehicles. Among various deep learning-based perception methods, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) stand out for their ability to deliver high performance without requiring manually crafted features. Consequently, deep learning has become a cornerstone technology for Environmental Perception (EP). This paper provides a survey of deep learning techniques applied to pixel-level computer vision tasks in EP, with a specific focus on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We review state-of-the-art approaches, detailing their architectures and losses. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive evaluation of deep network performance using Quantitative Analysis (QA) based on publicly available datasets. Our survey covers major object detection, semantic and semantic-instance segmentation, flow estimation, and depth estimation techniques. Finally, we discuss promising directions for future research in smart city vehicle environmental perception. Our aim is to offer readers a comprehensive perspective on recent advancements and to inspire innovative solutions for more effective smart city environmental perception. To achieve this, we provide a detailed taxonomy of deep learning methods for EP, outlining network architectures and characteristics in a way that allows for a clear comparison with existing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we perform a QA-based comparison of existing networks across object detection, flow estimation, and depth estimation tasks. We hope this survey equips researchers at all career stages with a robust perspective on deep learning techniques for smart city vehicle EP. To further assist, we have compiled supplementary materials, including a GitHub repository and a Qt-based desktop application, available via the link provided in the source. These tools utilize a taxonomy to visually compare network architectures, enabling readers to quickly comprehend how different networks operate. This study employs a coordinate space renormalization group method where block impurities are uniform balls or irregularly shaped clusters, characterized by their average linear size. The flow equations for the running coupling constants are derived up to the third order in the impurity concentration. Consequently, the critical exponent for the impurity scattering rate and the scaling behavior near the Lifshitz point depend on the average linear size of the clusters. Finally, our theoretical predictions are compared with prior Monte Carlo simulations, which serve as a benchmark for specific special cases. In the absence of such comparisons, it remains uncertain whether the third cumulant is correctly accounted for in the Monte Carlo renormalization group approach. This work underscores the necessity of including the third cumulant. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the concentration-dependent scaling law, previously reported in prior Monte Carlo studies, is inaccurate. Instead, a generalized scaling law is proposed, which aligns with the predictions of the present renormalization group theory. This scaling law applies to the temperature dependence of the specific heat, the density dependence of the specific heat amplitude, and the scaling behavior of the specific heat near the Lifshitz point. In all these instances, the theory predicts that the relevant critical exponent varies with the average linear size of the extended impurities. This dependence on cluster size constitutes a distinct and essential prediction of the current theoretical framework. It is hoped that this scaling law will serve as a valuable tool for experimentally testing the validity of the third cumulant. Additionally, the novel role of the third cumulant in the context of the Lifshitz point is emphasized. Our methodology is also applicable to other impurity systems, such as the Anderson model. Despite their ability to exhibit complex behaviors, individual plant cells lack the sophistication found in animal cells. This contrast raises the question of how multicellular organisms develop behavioral complexity. Recent findings indicate that this capability arises through simple adjustments in gene expression within individual cells, which collectively influence systemic reactions to external stimuli. This review outlines the technologies and methodologies driving these discoveries and proposes future directions for research. By integrating classical plant biology with modern single-cell analytical tools, we can uncover fundamental principles governing multicellular life across all domains. Consequently, these insights may yield new materials and systems capable of demonstrating adaptive behaviors in non-living contexts. Furthermore, these principles may offer theoretical and mathematical frameworks to better understand the evolutionary transition from unicellular to multicellular organisms. Ultimately, this knowledge could enhance our ability to sustain plant life in challenging environments, such as those affected by climate change, thereby supporting human civilization. Additionally, these theoretical advances may significantly impact the design of synthetic multicellular systems with non-living applications. Finally, these insights could transform the way we visualize and comprehend the organism as a unified entity. This article serves as a companion to a Feature Issue of *Cell Systems*, which synthesizes recent advancements in plant multicellularity and explores their broader implications. Specifically, it addresses the second theme, examining the transition from unicellular to multicellular life. The issue includes a model comparing univariate and bivariate adaptive dynamics in adaptive walks across heterogeneous landscapes, while the accompanying perspective outlines the future research landscape. This overview underscores the emerging understanding of how modifications to single-cell behaviors enable complex systemic responses. It posits that engineering these single-cell properties could facilitate the creation of useful synthetic multicellular systems. The following overview is structured into three parts: (i) historical context, (ii) current research, and (iii) future directions. **Part I: Historical Context.** We begin by reviewing the historical development of plant multicellularity concepts, highlighting key contributions from both animal and plant biology. This section examines how these perspectives have evolved over time and identifies remaining gaps in understanding the transition from unicellular to multicellular life. **Part II: Current Research.** We then summarize recent studies demonstrating how changes in single-cell behaviors drive complex systemic responses. This segment highlights the technologies and methods enabling these insights, illustrating how they can be generalized across species. It also explores the diversity of plant multicellular systems and their applications in other multicellular organisms. **Part III: Future Directions.**

Specifically, we show that the multi-point joint law of CFT field values on a disk matches the law obtained by sampling a CFT field value on the sphere and then wrapping the resulting tree via the Schramm-Werner conformal tangent circle process. Our approach begins by analyzing the conformal welding of two infinite cone LQG surfaces and subsequently reconstructing the original LQG disk through quantum gravitational time reversal. Finally, our proof for the isotropic cone case relies on the identification of isotropic cone measure with the uniformization of an LQG disk via the recent Bowers-Hahn theorem. All integrals involved converge absolutely. Additionally, we identify specific instances where the LQG disk can be reconstructed from the cone via time reversal without requiring further integration. Through these methods, we successfully achieve the proof. Our results also indicate that the uniformization technique characterizes the conformal welding of two infinite cone LQG surfaces and potentially recovers the original cone from a sampled tree. This scenario corresponds to strong couplings between spin-1 particles on honeycomb lattices, where the spin-1 Bose-Hubbard model effectively transforms into the spin-3/2 Heisenberg model. At particular points within the parameter space, the ground state of the spin-3/2 Heisenberg model is anticipated to be a chiral spin liquid, grounded on the hypothesis that the spin-5/2 ground state shares the same topological order. Furthermore, we report on two promising real materials, YbMgGaO$_4$ and Cu$_2$Te$_5$, where the spin-3/2 Bose-Hubbard model is expected to be near a chiral spin liquid phase. This suggests that both compounds serve as viable candidates for observing chiral spin liquid phases. Additionally, we explore the impact of weak magnetic fields on the spin-3/2 system, revealing that the ground state evolves into a gapped pseudogap state within the chiral spin liquid phase, where the energy gap can be adjusted across a broad spectrum by varying the external magnetic field. Finally, we examine the specific point-group symmetries of the spin-3/2 system, which suggest the possibility of a topologically distinct phase compatible with $C_2$ symmetry but exhibiting no chiral edge states, thereby representing a novel phase of matter. In this respect, our findings align with recent theoretical predictions regarding symmetry-protected topological phases in kagome lattices. Overall, our study provides fresh theoretical insights into the search for chiral spin liquid phases. These phases are potentially realizable in real materials where spin-1 particles dominate, enabling the observation of topological order without the need for external magnetic fields. This research extends our understanding beyond the standard spin-1/2 framework, offering new perspectives on chiral spin liquid phases and their search. In this context, our study holds significant importance. Given the current surge in experimental interest in spin-3/2 real materials, our theoretical predictions offer fresh inspiration for the ongoing pursuit of chiral spin liquid phases. Our results underscore the potential for discovering chiral spin liquid phases in spin-3/2 systems, presenting a new avenue for investigation. Through the spin-3/2 Bose-Hubbard model, our study opens new avenues for exploring the chiral spin liquid phase. We believe this research will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing search for chiral spin liquid phases.

Unlike standard dense networks, these Bayesian models offer robust uncertainty assessments, addressing significant challenges in both machine learning and scientific disciplines. Although the scientific community increasingly recognizes and utilizes uncertainties, implementing them effectively remains difficult; even with recent advancements, practical application for astronomers is still complex and non-trivial. This paper introduces a comprehensive overview of methodological approaches for calculating uncertainties in astronomical machine learning tasks. Using a case study of classifying Fermi-LAT sources, we evaluate and benchmark various techniques. On one hand, we examine both parametric and non-parametric Bayesian neural network approaches, offering the first comparison of these two methods in this context and demonstrating their complementary value. On the other hand, we incorporate two additional widely adopted strategies: deep ensembles and Monte Carlo (MC) drops. By leveraging the recent FastMCDroppy package, we perform a systematic comparison of MC cubes and MC drops, highlighting the superior performance and practicality of the latter. Our findings indicate that ensembles and MC drops yield superior accuracy and reliability compared to MC cubes. Ultimately, our comparative analysis reveals that combining MC drops with MC cubes surpasses the performance of both parametric and non-parametric methods, suggesting that uncertainty estimation in machine learning benefits from hybrid techniques. These concepts and their implementation are broadly applicable. Beyond classifying Fermi-LAT sources, our work offers a general framework for uncertainty modeling in machine learning. This is demonstrated through an extension to classical binary classification using the MNIST dataset, empirically validating that uncertainty estimates from MC drops exceed those from MC cubes, and that MC drops significantly outperform MC cubes in both scenarios. Our comprehensive comparison underscores the necessity of testing and validating all available methods to achieve optimal performance. Finally, our results provide a practical, empirical foundation for future research and development in uncertainty estimation for machine learning in astronomy. The accompanying GitHub repository contains all datasets, implementations, and discussions to facilitate further exploration and validation. Specifically, it will assist practitioners in understanding uncertainty estimation, testing various techniques and their combinations, and adapting methods to their own datasets and problems. This work represents a significant step toward making uncertainty estimation more accessible for machine learning in astronomy. Furthermore, our extensive discussion serves as a valuable resource for understanding current modeling approaches and future research directions. We conclude that uncertainty estimation using MC drops represents a state-of-the-art technique for uncertainty modeling in machine learning. Building upon our prior findings, which demonstrated that Cross-Domain Alignment (CSA) significantly boosts the performance of high-capacity, high-dimensional neural networks, Action-CS extends this approach further. Unlike reinforcement learning methods focused on specific domains, such as locomotion or games, Action-CSA applies to any control problem and offers clear interpretability, ensuring reliable execution even in unfamiliar scenarios. This paper explores both physical simulations and real-world deployments of Action-CSA. We demonstrate that it facilitates the coordination of multiple robots for multi-object manipulation and enables human-robot collaboration, achieving results comparable to reinforcement learning policies. On a physical platform with two PR2 robots and two humans, Action-CSA successfully executed multi-object manipulation tasks up to ten times faster than human operators alone. Similarly, it accelerated a human walker's locomotion by four times compared to baseline policies. These experiments validate that Action-CSA is highly effective for controlling multiple sources across diverse, realistic domains. Comprehensive videos of Action-CSA deployments are available at https://csail.github.io/action-csa/. We posit that Action-CSA represents a practical solution for multiple source control, opening new avenues for applications in everyday life. Additionally, we release our Python open-source library, https://github.com/csail-visionlab/ReCSALab, which encompasses not only Action-CSA but also reinforcement learning techniques and visualization tools for multiple source control. This paper investigates grant-free communication under receive-side constraints, specifically targeting scenarios with limited receiver capabilities. We propose a framework utilizing code-division multiple access (CDMA) combined with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), employing graph neural networks (GNNs) at the receiver to facilitate joint detection and path loss estimation. Leveraging GNNs offers significant advantages over conventional methods by reducing complexity, enhancing performance, and ensuring adaptability. At the transmitter, no specific designs or features are required. The proposed GNN-based framework is evaluated across both orthogonal and non-orthogonal CDMA, as well as narrowband and wideband environments. In all cases, the GNN-based approach demonstrates superior characteristics regarding bit error rate (BER), channel estimation accuracy, and computational complexity. Our results indicate that the proposed GNN-based framework achieves significant gains in BER and channel estimation relative to baseline MF-based schemes, while also offering substantial complexity reductions, particularly over non-orthogonal access channels and in wideband scenarios. Extensive simulations confirm the effectiveness, complexity efficiency, and channel adaptability of the proposed GNN framework, which require no specific features from the coded access scheme. Consequently, this GNN-based framework serves as an optimal solution for grant-free access, delivering superior channel estimation and BER performance with minimal complexity, irrespective of transmit-time or frequency domain orthogonality. The proposed framework further enhances channel adaptability through the message passing mechanism, which allows for the concurrent processing of multiple inputs to produce multi-dimensional outputs. Finally, the design demonstrates robustness against variations in network parameters, such as the number of active devices, without requiring any modifications to the GNN architecture. In essence, the GNN-based joint detector/path loss estimator significantly outperforms baseline designs across diverse network scenarios, featuring a novel architecture that is both channel-adaptive and parameter-efficient, making it an ideal solution for massive machine-type communications. With this count defined, the universal access structure represents the most comprehensive configuration, containing participants in every possible Boolean combination of these minimal sets. Since every access structure is a subset of the universal structure sharing the same number of minimal qualified subsets, universal structures exhibit the maximum complexity for a given number of minimal sets. In this study, we numerically investigate palm tree solitons within the two-dimensional (2D) Lugiato-Lefever equation (LLE), which serves as a canonical model for optical cavities driven by coherent light. Our results demonstrate the emergence of palm tree solitons at low input detuning through a primary bifurcation from input resonance patterns (IRP) featuring Palmquist-type symmetry breaking, where two fundamental spots develop within one period cell alongside symmetric side lobes. At the transition point, these side lobes are positioned at the system boundaries. As the detuning varies, these boundaries shift within the toroidal domain, causing the side lobes to wind around the periodic boundaries and ultimately merge with the main spots, resulting in the formation of palm tree solitons. We characterize these structures by counting their side lobes and analyzing their symmetry. Furthermore, we examine how higher-order palm tree solitons arise from primary ones via secondary symmetry-breaking bifurcations, a process that eliminates additional side lobes. The optical field of the palm tree soliton exhibits 4-fold symmetry, in contrast to the 2-fold symmetry of the IRP, and this secondary symmetry breaking is analyzed using amplitude-based localized structures (Lz). Finally, we discuss the significance of these highly stable palm tree solitons and their robustness against perturbations. Given their optical nature and stability, they are promising for the all-optical storage of multi-bit information, where each bit corresponds to a distinct localized optical structure. Additionally, we demonstrate that primary and various palm tree solitons can be effectively controlled using a single control beam.

Palm tree solitons, characterized by a central spot surrounded by a ring of symmetric side lobes, are identified both numerically and analytically within the 2D LLE framework. Analyzing their symmetries and stability reveals that they are highly robust against perturbations, including those with complex structures. These robust structures hold promise for all-optical multi-bit storage and can be manipulated using a single control beam.

Their formation involves a primary bifurcation from input resonance patterns and a secondary breaking of 2-fold symmetry. Experimental and numerical studies confirm their high stability across diverse physical systems

Their core learning mechanism relies on message passing, where nodes iteratively gather information from neighbors to refine their own states. This process is typically realized through aggregating neighbors' features and appending them to the node's existing state. GNNs have demonstrated remarkable success across various graph machine learning tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. The results confirm that the local-global architecture significantly improves the model's ability to capture graph structure and enhances overall performance. In this paper, we introduce a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework designed to teach multi-fingered robotic hands how to grasp diverse objects using minimal training data and without requiring hand object configurations during training. Each finger is equipped with its own agent that learns to apply contact forces to achieve cooperative grasping. a novel approach for classifying lung sound recordings, specifically targeting wheezing and crackles.

**Background:** Classifying lung sounds is a vital component of automated auscultation, yet it remains challenging due to the requirement for specialized medical expertise and the rarity of specific sound occurrences. While spectrogram-based methods using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown efficacy in this domain, there is a lack of clear guidance on optimal network architecture design. This absence of guidance stems from insufficient understanding of the relationship between the problem's characteristics and suitable CNN architectures.

**Methodology:** This study investigates the impact of CNN architecture on the performance of a sound classification system by examining three distinct scenarios: a) a shallow CNN, b) a deep CNN, and (c) an ensemble of deep CNNs utilizing diverse augmentation techniques. The evaluation was conducted on a public dataset containing 10,752 recordings, comprising 6,858 instances of wheezing, 268 of crackles, and 368 normal cases.

**Results:** Our findings indicate that an ensemble of deep CNNs with diverse augmentation strategies yields superior results compared to both shallow and standard deep CNNs, as well as rule-of-thumb-based designs. Specifically, the ensemble-based system achieved an accuracy of 86.8%, an improvement of 6.2% over the shallow CNN (80.6%) and 3.8% over the deep CNN (83.0%). Additionally, this ensemble approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, surpassing their accuracy by approximately 10%.

**Conclusion:** We have demonstrated that an ensemble of deep CNNs employing diverse augmentation strategies produces a more robust classifier than either a shallow CNN or a standalone deep CNN. Furthermore, by evaluating various public datasets, our system achieves significant performance gains over existing state-of-the-art approaches. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/ahmetkayaci/CNNEnsemble_LungSoundClassification. The lead author will present these findings at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP).

The proposed method operates through three key stages: first, a distillation process is applied to transfer complete information from the teacher model to the student; second, channel distillation is conducted to enable the student to identify redundant filters within each channel group and retain only those with significant information; third, channel groups contributing most to the knowledge shared between the teacher and student are prioritized to maximize information retention in the sparse architecture. Extensive experiments across various architectures demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantial improvements in both accuracy and model size. Specifically, on the ImageNet dataset, our approach attains a top-1 accuracy of 78.7% with a 44.5% model size reduction, outperforming the state-of-the-art Distill-Prune method which achieves 78.1% accuracy with the same degree of sparsity. Furthermore, on COCO, the proposed method reaches a mAP of 68.1% with a 44.0% model size reduction, surpassing the best-performing Baseline Pruning method's mAP of 67.7%. These results confirm the efficacy and practical value of the proposed method for high-performance, lightweight model deployment. Currently, secure information transmission is constrained by the fundamental no-cloning theorem of quantum mechanics to the point-to-point quantum key distribution channel. Consequently, quantum entanglement exhibits a strong correlation between observation and communication. This study investigates the quantum communication methods employed by financial institutions to transmit financial data regarding financial instruments. We demonstrate that HFT can be achieved through the quantum internet via two distinct protocols: direct transmission of financial data encoded in the quantum basis, and indirect transmission utilizing classical data encoded in the non-quantum basis. For the first protocol, if the quantum network's success rate reaches 50%, the quantum-based trading strategy will match classical trading performance. In the second protocol, a significant correlation exists between classical financial channels and trading profits, meaning HFT will outperform low-frequency trading. Thus, financial institutions should adopt HFT methods when transmitting financial information in financial data. Furthermore, we observe that quantum communication is not strictly required for HFT; instead, high-frequency trading can be achieved through high-frequency information transmission leveraging the quantum network. Additionally, due to the quantum memory bottleneck, we conclude that while quantum communication is beneficial for HFT, it is not strictly necessary. Finally, we explore the relationship between the quantum network and the classical communication channel, demonstrating that the more financial data transmitted through the quantum network, the weaker the classical communication channel becomes. This confirms the existence of a competition between the quantum and classical communication channels. Finally, we prove that the larger the quantum success rate, the smaller the classical communication channel's capacity, which is 1-log_2(1-p). This indicates that the quantum channel is a quantum complement channel, where an increase in the quantum channel's success rate leads to a decrease in the classical communication channel's capacity. In this context, HFT can be viewed as a classical communication channel, implying that enhancing the quantum channel's success rate may negatively impact HFT. Therefore, financial institutions should not blindly pursue HFT, as blindly transmitting financial data via HFT through a quantum network may be counterproductive. We address two specific cases: first, when every agent possesses sufficient data to estimate their valuation with high precision, and second, when only a subset of agents has adequate data while the remainder has only access to prior distributions. Our findings indicate that the second scenario yields significantly worse outcomes. In the optimal mechanism for the first case, agents with the highest valuations secure the items, with each paying a price equal to their respective marginal contribution; consequently, agents with sufficient data are overwhelmingly likely to win when endowing agents with insufficient data results in lower valuations.

We propose a new mechanism designed to close this performance gap. Its core concept involves allocating a portion of the $k$ items to agents with insufficient data; specifically, a deterministic number of items is assigned to a single agent with the highest valuation among those with insufficient data. We demonstrate that, under our mechanism, the agents with the highest valuations still win, but every agent with insufficient data has a positive probability of securing at least one item. Furthermore, these allocated items contribute to satisfying demand among agents with insufficient data, thereby increasing their overall revenue. We establish existence proofs for the optimal mechanism in both scenarios and derive existence theorems for the mechanism we propose. Finally, we present numerical results confirming that our mechanism outperforms the optimal mechanism in the case where agents with insufficient data have lower valuations. These results also reveal that allocating fewer items to insufficient agents does not necessarily reduce their revenue. Furthermore, simulations indicate that deterministic mechanisms can perform closely to the optimal deterministic mechanism.

Additionally, we demonstrate how to parameterize a typical scene object—such as a person—using an observed view, even with minimal supervision. Our approach relies primarily on supervision from an existing 3D detector and a 3D bounding box derived from the input image, enabling the model to generalize effectively to novel objects. We present the initial COCO 3D dataset, containing 3D models for over 4,000 object categories, and show that our model can generate high-quality, diverse animations with only a single image as input. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/AsadKhwajaCVC/COCO-3D-Deformable-Objects. We also release the modeled person via an API. The detected, rich 3D object models, now available for the first time, offer novel, promising, and broad novel opportunities for multi-view reconstruction, 3D object detection, contactless monitoring, augmented and virtual reality, and the creation of the first 3D deformable object datasets. The COCO-3D object detection leaderboard can be found at https://coco-det.com/leaderboards?task=person. The project is also available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.09929. we investigate the connection between initial geometric anisotropies and anisotropic flow within relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Specifically, we examine how elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular flow ($v_3$) vary with collision system and centrality. Our findings indicate that the ratio of triangular flow to elliptic flow ($v_3/v_2$) follows the same centrality dependence across all systems, including Cu+Cu, Au+Au, U+U, Pb+Pb, and Xe+Xe. This ratio is governed by fluctuations in the initial triangularity ($\epsilon_3$) relative to ellipticity ($\epsilon_2$), which in turn depend on the participant geometry and multiplicity of the specific collision system. Our results demonstrate that the initial ratio of triangular to elliptic anisotropy, $\rho_{32} = (\epsilon_3/\langle\epsilon_2\rangle)_0$, which dictates the $v_3/v_2$ ratio, remains independent of the final system, varying solely with final centrality. This conclusion holds across a wide temperature range achieved by different colliding systems. Furthermore, we show that the $v_3/v_2$ ratio is largely insensitive to the equation of state (EoS). These results confirm that the geometric nature of the initial quark-gluon plasma (QGP) system depends exclusively on the participant configuration of the collision. Consequently, our data can serve to constrain uncertainties regarding the initial condition models of the QGP. Furthermore, by applying a model-independent approach, we determine that the evolution of the QGP is essentially insensitive to the EoS, given that the $\rho_{32}$ ratio remains independent of the specific colliding systems. Finally, our results indicate that the quark coalescence mechanism is essential for accurately describing the $v_3/v_2$ ratio in this scenario. This conclusion remains robust against variations in the transport time and quark recombination probability. These results also highlight a potential role for the quark coalescence mechanism in enhancing $p_T$-differential $v_3/v_2$ ratios observed in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC. In summary, the $v_3/v_2$ ratio serves as a valuable tool for probing the QGP, as it is independent of uncertainties in energy density, transport time, equation of state, and quark recombination probability, depending only on the geometric characteristics of the initial partonic system

SyROF comprises a rapid decompilation framework capable of translating decoupled pseudo-code specific to target environments into standard ROS-based code for general-purpose robotic platforms. Leveraging this system, we developed a high-throughput deployment pipeline that configures, connects, and data-log simultaneously the entire deployment code, significantly reducing testing time for deployment scenarios. Utilizing SyRORO, we executed 7 deployment scenarios involving up to 20 robots in parallel, achieving up to a 90-fold reduction in testing time compared to conventional methods that deploy code on each robot sequentially. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this testbed streamlines the validation of deployment code within a formal verification framework, ensuring functional correctness before physical hardware implementation. Our objective is to use SyROF to deliver robust, verified, and formalized deployment code for deployment on real robotic platforms. This approach guarantees that deployed systems are free from bugs, enhancing our safety and security posture. Finally, we argue that such a framework serves as a vital component of the next generation of self-deploying robotic systems. We have made SyROF publicly accessible to accelerate research in self-deploying robotic swarms. The code repository can be found at: https://github.com/syrorof. This paper details our experience deploying syROF and the steps required to integrate it into related research. However, cloud services are vulnerable to attacks that compromise user privacy; specifically, inference attacks allow adversaries to deduce sensitive attributes from released data. Additionally, many cloud-infrastructure devices, such as SDN switches, possess SUID (Set User ID) permissions, which grant root access to users, further risking system security and user privacy if breached. While valid for dimensions up to 117, recent findings by Karrenberger demonstrate that the maximum diameter can reach $n - d + \Omega(n^{1/6})$. Karrenberger's method involves a local search algorithm that may require up to $n - d + \alpha$ steps to find an optimal solution, accompanied by corresponding perturbed objective functions. Building on this, our work presents a randomized algorithm capable of optimizing any $d$-dimensional polytope defined by $n$ inequalities with high probability using no more than $n - d + \alpha + \beta$ iterations, where $\alpha$ represents the overestimation of Karrenberger's example and $\beta$ the overestimation introduced by our algorithm. This algorithm operates randomly, allowing for multiple independent runs to potentially reduce the probability of failure. A key component is a novel pipeline that, with high probability, identifies a perturbed objective function achievable via at most $\beta$ iterations of the local search, starting from a vertex distinct from the global optimum. The primary contribution lies in the design and analysis of this pipeline, along with an in-depth discussion of the problem's parameters. This approach represents the first randomized algorithm addressing the optimization of general linear programs in polytopes, with its complexity determined by the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Furthermore, the algorithm's design is robust, facilitating the synthesis of various general purpose local search algorithms. We also explore the relationship between the pipeline, the original problem, and the identified perturbed problem, highlighting the non-triviality of this relationship. Furthermore, by employing a graded extension of Quillen–Suslin theory, we establish a corresponding result for graded rings. These findings are applied to analyze polynomial extensions of generalized matrix rings, as well as graded quadratic and unitary matrix rings, thereby demonstrating the torsion-free property in their nil-groups. All proofs are established over rings of characteristic zero or rings containing the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$. To address rings of characteristic $p>0$, we outline several potential approaches, contingent upon further investigation. The primary objective is to quantify the impact of off-shell and non-resonant effects on the shapes of differential distributions, which are essential for extracting the top quark mass via the template fit method. To achieve this, we utilize a recently developed tool, PP2F, that integrates the full tree-level matrix element with phase-space mapping into a unified, xactyla 2, fast, and flexible output format, streamlining comparisons with experimental data. We demonstrate that the nW approximation introduces substantial distortions in distributions sensitive to new physics beyond the Standard Model, as well as in distributions used for the top quark mass measurement. However, the peak of the missing transverse energy spectrum remains a notable exception. Additionally, we examine the utility of shape variables for determining the w boson mass in the t-channel single-top production process. Our findings indicate that certain W boson mass-related observables can be accurately modeled using the narrow width approximation, while others in the single-top process do not. We also discuss the significance of incorporating these effects into the template fit procedure for mass reconstruction. Finally, we outline the current status of a template fit for the w boson mass using PP2F results, alongside a sketch of a similar fit for the top quark mass. This report is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a brief summary of the parton-level calculation implementation in PP2F and the resulting xactyla 2 output format; Section 3 presents detailed comparisons of various distributions for both ttbar single and single-top production; Section 4 details a template fit for the W boson mass and investigates top-quark background effects; and Section 5 describes a template fit for the top quark mass, including a first attempt at including W boson off-shell effects. In each section, we contrast our full results with those from the narrow width approximation, discussing the magnitude of observed differences and their implications. We also illustrate how these effects influence the final template fit and the resulting uncertainty in the extracted parameter. Within the template fit, we explain how various components contribute to the total uncertainty and suggest strategies to reduce them. We conclude by summarizing our findings and proposing future research directions. An updated version of this report, titled "A ctacle, fast output format for top-quark analyses," is available on the project's GitHub repository: https://github.com/PP2Fproject/pp2f

This approach accelerates the generation of new solutions by reducing the time required to evaluate them. The extent of acceleration achieved varies based on the specific problem, its size, solution complexity, and the characteristics of the parallel hardware used. This study examines four state-of-the-art PEA implementations across a variety of standard computational tasks to determine if the observed acceleration aligns with expectations from the parallel environment.
